item.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+path-dependent+preference+formation+in+RL+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts.\", \"abstract\": \"The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant (redSR), particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts - and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.\", \"doi\": \"10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873\", \"pmid\": \"42905773\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13716319\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"…

This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.\", \"doi\": \"10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873\", \"pmid\": \"42905773\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13716319\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13716319\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13716319?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Risk-aware tactical path planning in partially observable environments via trajectory-value factorized recurrent PPO.\", \"abstract\": \"Operating unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in partially observable battlefields requires balancing movement efficiency and proxy risk exposure. Traditional shortest-path algorithms typically struggle here, as their use of purely geometric distances often yields tactically vulnerable routes. We confront this challenge by introducing a risk-aware path-planning framework driven by Trajectory-Value Factorized Recurrent Proximal Policy Optimization (TVF-RPPO). Our integrated navigation pipeline combines a SwiftFormer perception unit to map terrain-specific costs and risks with a GRU-based belief state that continuously tracks observation history. Unlike standard approaches that fuse competing goals into a single scalar reward, TVF-RPPO explicitly splits value estimation into separate time-efficiency and risk-avoidance channels. This structural shift is the key mechanism that enables the network to efficiently regulate speed and safety. During our 2D evaluations involving static, dynamic, and active threat scenarios, the technique reduced proxy risk exposure compared with baseline planners while maintaining competitive mission-completion performance in the tested simulation scenarios. A major practical benefit of this factorization is its adjustability. By simply tuning a single risk-weight parameter during inference, the UGV can immediately switch between cautious and aggressive maneuvers without additional training.\", \"doi\": \"10.1038/s41598-026-54500-5\", \"pmid\": \"42191805\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13434189\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54500-5\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13434189\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13434189?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Chaotic Itinerancy in Collective Behaviour Emerging from Active Inference: A Multi-Agent Model of Trust and Empowerment Dynamics in Theatre Workshops.\", \"abstract\": \"Chaotic itinerancy-irregular switching among metastable collective states-provides a dynamical substrate for flexible social coordination, yet its mechanistic origin in multi-agent systems remains unclear. We present a multi-agent Active Inference model in which chaotic itinerancy emerges from Expected Free Energy minimisation without outcome-level social priors. Agents select actions to minimise Expected Free Energy while updating preferences through a precision-gated learning mechanism modulated by interpersonal trust. Hill-function nonlinearity in state transitions creates bistable \\\"affordance landscapes\\\" that gate behavioural mode switching. Simulations with small number of agents on an Erdős-Rényi trust network reveal spontaneous alternation among multiple metastable behavioural clusters, heavy-tailed dwell-time distributions, and sign-changing finite-time Lyapunov exponents-three hallmarks of chaotic itinerancy. Crucially, replacing Hill-function dynamics with linear transitions reduces the chaotic-itinerancy detection rate from 80% to 20%, demonstrating that nonlinear affordance structure is necessary for generating metastable switching. We further show that agents with simplified internal models of the world sustain richer itinerant dynamics as a group than \\\"perfect-foresight\\\" agents, suggesting that bounded rationality may be functionally advantageous for maintaining behavioural flexibility. These results establish active inference as a principled framework for modelling chaotic itinerancy in social systems and offer a computational account of trust-mediated collective transitions observed in theatre workshops and group dynamics.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/e28050491\", \"pmid\": \"42187906\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13205385\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/e28050491\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13205385\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13205385?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"TrajGNN-RL: Adaptive Mobile Sink Intelligence for Lifetime-Aware Wireless Sensor Networks.\", \"abstract\": \"Mobile wireless sensor networks require adaptive routing and sink mobility strategies to reduce energy imbalance, congestion, and communication delay. In this study, we propose a new method called TrajGNN-RL that combines the topology learning method based on a graph neural network with the deep reinforcement learning method to plan the trajectory of the mobile sink and route the packet in a coordinated manner. Dynamic communication graphs model the residual energy, link quality, neighborhood connectivity, and traffic conditions, and reinforcement learning optimizes the sink movement and forwarding decisions via a multi-objective approach. The graph changes during network operation to handle topology and traffic changes. The performance of the proposed routing scheme was compared with the performance of the evaluated routing schemes through experimental evaluation using varying numbers of sinks and varying sink mobility. The proposed TrajGNN-RL enhanced the normalized scores of the lifetime, energy efficiency, throughput, PkDel, routing reliability, and delay reduction by 98.34%, 97.86%, 98.12%, 98.57%, 98.83%, and 96.75%, respectively. The relative improvements in the normalized lifetime, energy efficiency, throughput, packet delivery ratio, and delay reduction, respectively, were around 1.47%, 1.55%, 0.68%, 1.19%, and 1.07%, compared to the best corresponding baseline used in the experiments.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/s26206444\", \"pmid\": \"42944307\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13709133\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/s26206444\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13709133\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13709133?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "fa2617becd81fe2ce90596962b57a39f1256e319ca7ed0f08b3b3425ddf5139a", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_formed_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873", "doi:10.1038/s41598-026-54500-5", "doi:10.3390/e28050491", "doi:10.3390/s26206444", "pmc:PMC13716319", "pmc:PMC13434189", "pmc:PMC13205385", "pmc:PMC13709133"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13716319", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13716319?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54500-5", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13434189", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13434189?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/e28050491", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13205385"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
